en: When the change is capable of affecting the core of enjoyment of the IOC, good faith requires communication oriented to what is essential, hierarchized and timed to the moment when the consumer can still understand the impact, react, decide and, if necessary, contest.<1>p. 657</1>

The very relational logic of good faith prevents the supplier from imposing unnecessary or malicious devices that turn the exercise of the right into a documentary via crucis or a game of clues.<1>p. 657</1>

This duty of qualified communication also prevents the platform from turning the consumer's silence, passivity or mere permanence in the environment into fictitious acceptance of relevant mutations.<1>p. 658</1>

Significant changes cannot be implemented through generic communications or communications structured to convert silence into fictitious acceptance, a practice considered abusive because it authorizes the unilateral modification of the content or quality of the performances after the contract is concluded <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1319-1320)</2>. Even when companies intend to use such mechanisms, they must ensure ample information and a reasonable period for the consumer, failing which they engage in exploitation of the passivity and practical dependence inherent in contracts of continuous performance <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 1319-1320)</4>.<5>p. 658</5>

The second mechanism is the preservation of minimum technical records. Total exposure of the system is not required, but rather a minimum documentary core, with the history of relevant versions, records of changes with functional impact, consent and decision-flow trails, transaction history, change communications and, where there is enforcement, that is, a sanction applied by the platform itself, the category applied, the reason and the consequence. The consumer does not need to know the engineering of the system, but needs to be able to demonstrate, and the protection bodies need to be able to verify, what happened in a legally relevant way.

What is required here is not a total exposure of the system, but a minimum documentary core: history of relevant versions; essential records of changes with functional impact; consent and decision-flow trails; history of relevant transactions; change communications; and, where there is enforcement, basic records of the decision event, such as the category applied, reason and consequence<1>p. 658</1>

The consumer does not need to know the full engineering of the system, but needs to be able to demonstrate — and the protection bodies need to be able to verify — what happened in a legally relevant way. Without this, the technical mutability of the service becomes an evidentiary safe-conduct, and the duty to inform degenerates into archival performance: a lot of paper for little verifiability.<1>p. 659</1>
How do you ask the judge for the right record?

The third mechanism is procedural and brings together preservation of evidence, production of documents and dynamic redistribution of the burden. Article 373, paragraph 1, of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC)<1><2>4</2></1> allows the judge to allocate the burden differently in the cases provided by law or in view of peculiarities of the case related to the impossibility or excessive difficulty of meeting the burden, or to the greater ease of obtaining proof of the contrary fact, provided it is done by a reasoned decision. This is the normal configuration of disputes over IOCs, in which logs, interface trails, change histories, sanction criteria and internal support communications are concentrated in the supplier, and redistribution appears, with support in the treatise by Benjamin, Marques and Bessa, as a technically adequate response to the structural asymmetry of evidence.

“Art. 373. The burden of proof lies: […] § 1 In the cases provided by law or in view of peculiarities of the case related to the impossibility or excessive difficulty of meeting the burden […] or to the greater ease of obtaining proof of the contrary fact, the judge may allocate the burden of proof differently, provided it is done by a reasoned decision […].” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2025]b)</2>.<3>p. 659</3>

In disputes over IOCs, this is precisely the normal configuration: logs, interface trails, change histories, sanction criteria, internal support communications and relevant technical records are concentrated in the supplier. Dynamic redistribution of the burden, therefore, does not arise as extravagant judicial benevolence, but as a technically adequate response to the structural asymmetry of evidence <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, p. 145; p. 184)</2>.<3>p. 659</3>

The most direct route to operate open auditability is the production of a document or thing under Articles 396 to 400 of the CPC<1><2>5</2></1>. Article 396 of the CPC<3><4>6</4></3> authorizes the judge to order the production of a document or thing in the possession of the party, and Article 397 of the CPC<5><6>7</6></5> requires the request to include the identification, as complete as possible, of the document, the purpose of the evidence and the circumstances indicating that it exists and is held by the opposing party. Hence the rule, surgical requests and not procedural fishing expeditions. Instead of all the data in the system, the consumer may request the history of relevant versions of a given item, the trail of screens shown at purchase, the minimum records of the specific transaction, the content of the change communication or the category and reason for the sanction applied.

In the same vein, the regime for the production of a document or thing provided for in Articles 396 to 400 of the CPC<1><2>5</2></1> offers the most direct route to operationalize open auditability.<3>p. 659</3>
“Art. 396. The judge may order the party to produce a document or thing in its possession.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2025]b)</2>.<3>p. 659</3>

“Art. 397. The request made by the party shall contain: I - the identification, as complete as possible, of the document or thing; II - the purpose of the evidence, indicating the facts related to the document or thing; III - the circumstances on which the requesting party relies to assert that the document or thing exists and is in the possession of the opposing party.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2025]b)</2>.<3>p. 660</3>
This allows surgical requests, not procedural fishing expeditions.<1>p. 660</1>

Instead of generically requesting “all the data in the system”, the consumer may request, for example, the history of relevant versions of a given item, the trail of screens shown along the purchase path, the minimum records of the specific transaction, the content of the change communication or the category and reason for the sanction applied.<1>p. 660</1>

If the supplier denies having the document, Article 398 of the CPC<1><2>8</2></1> allows the requesting party to prove, by any means, that the statement is not true. Under Article 399 of the CPC<3><4>9</4></3>, refusal is not admitted if the respondent has a legal obligation to produce, if it has referred to the document in the proceedings in order to constitute evidence or if the document is common to the parties. In the face of unjustified refusal, Article 400 of the CPC<5><6>10</6></5> authorizes the judge to accept as true the facts that the document would serve to prove. These are the guarantees that answer the formulas well known in platform litigation, such as that the information no longer exists, that it is internal-use data or that there is no way to reconstruct the procedure.

“Art. 398. The respondent shall reply within the 5 (five) days following its summons. Sole paragraph. If the respondent states that it does not possess the document or thing, the judge shall allow the requesting party to prove, by any means, that the statement does not correspond to the truth. Art. 399. The judge shall not admit the refusal if: I - the respondent has a legal obligation to produce; II - the respondent has referred to the document or thing, in the proceedings, in order to constitute evidence; III - the document, by its content, is common to the parties.”<1>p. 660</1>

“Art. 400. In deciding the request, the judge shall accept as true the facts that, by means of the document or thing, the party intended to prove […].” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2025]b)</2>.<3>p. 660</3>

If the supplier denies possessing the document, art. [...] allows the requesting party to demonstrate by other means that the denial is untrue; if the refusal is unjustified, art. [...] authorizes the judge to accept as true the facts that the document would serve to prove <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2025]b)</2>.<3>p. 660</3>

In platform-related disputes, the procedural guarantees meet the need to react to generic answers such as “we no longer have such information”, “this is internal-use data”, “this information is not accessible to the public” or “we are unable to reconstruct the procedure”.<1>p. 660</1>

The evidentiary arm is linked to the duty of clarification. The supplier does not fulfill its role by throwing information into the environment, because it must demonstrate, when questioned, that it informed adequately, that it exercised the power of alteration regularly and that the impact was compatible with the promised performance, and Bruno Miragem places this demonstration within the supplier's own burden. Miragem further treats greater risk without sufficiently conspicuous information as an informational defect, whose nonexistence the supplier must demonstrate by express legal allocation of the burden, and from this follows, with support in the same author, the rule for the platform. Where there is a relevant mutation whose intelligibility depends on data controlled by the company, it is for the company to demonstrate the nonexistence of the defect or nonconformity, and not for the consumer to prove in the dark what happened in an environment the consumer does not control.

The supplier does not fulfill its role merely by throwing information into the environment; it must also demonstrate, when questioned, that it informed adequately, that it exercised its power of alteration regularly and that the impact produced was compatible with the promised performance. Demonstrating compliance with these duties forms part of its own burden of proof <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 412)</2>.<3>p. 660</3>

Where there is greater risk without sufficiently conspicuous information, an informational defect is configured, and the absence of adequate clarification prevents the consumer from taking the necessary precautions. Even when the supplier seeks to rule out its liability, it will be for it to demonstrate the nonexistence of the defect, by express legal allocation of the burden of proof <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 488)</2>.<3>p. 643</3>

Where there is greater risk without sufficiently conspicuous information, an informational defect or a relevant mutation whose intelligibility depends on data controlled by the company, it will be for the company to demonstrate the nonexistence of the defect or nonconformity, and not for the consumer to prove in the dark what happened inside the environment the consumer does not control <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 488)</2>.<3>p. 660</3>
Where does the disagreement over the burden of proof lie?

The reference provision is Article 6, item VIII, of the CDC<1><2>11</2></1>, which ensures the facilitation of the defense of the consumer's rights, including through the reversal of the burden of proof. The disagreement lies in how to apply the guarantee to the digital environment. Mariana de Moraes Palmeira, starting from digital vulnerability, argues for the universalization of the consumer's hyposufficiency in that environment and, by derivation, for the reversal of the burden as a rule, ope legis, that is, by force of the law itself, and not only ope judicis, by the judge's decision in the case. The gain is real, a concrete protective response above all on the evidentiary plane, but it has a limit, because the consequence is organized en bloc, from the global perception of a hostile environment, without isolating the specific mechanism that produces the asymmetry. The alternative is to shift the ground to the mechanism, and then evidence comes to require preservation of trails, verifiable transparency and rational redistribution of the burden.

“Art. 6. The basic rights of the consumer are: I - the protection of life, health and safety against the risks caused by practices in the supply of products and services considered dangerous or harmful; III - adequate and clear information about the different products and services […]; IV - protection against misleading and abusive advertising, coercive or unfair commercial methods, as well as against abusive practices and clauses […]; VI - the effective prevention and redress of pecuniary and moral damages […]; VIII - the facilitation of the defense of their rights, including through the reversal of the burden of proof […].” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2022])</2>.<3>p. 511</3>

The dogmatic operability of the competing category appears clearly when a concrete procedural consequence is drawn from it: the universalization of the consumer's hyposufficiency in the digital environment and, by derivation, of the reversal of the burden of proof.<1>p. 593</1>

This consequence is reaffirmed when it is argued that the protection currently offered by the CDC and the LGPD is insufficient in the face of the new bases of relationship in the digital environment, which is why digital vulnerability and the corresponding hyposufficiency should be affirmed in universal terms, with reversal of the burden of proof ope legis, and not only ope judicis <1>Palmeira</1><2>(Palmeira, 2022, p. 234)</2>. The gain of this formulation is clear: it offers a concrete protective response, above all on the evidentiary plane. The limit, however, appears in the same movement. The central legal consequence drawn from the category tends to be organized en bloc, through one large general effect, which confirms its strength as a comprehensive diagnosis, but also its more global and aggregating character.<3>p. 593</3>

But the label “digital vulnerability” or its close equivalents works, most of the time, better as a synthesis of a scenario than as an isolator of the legally central mechanism. Sometimes it produces a concrete protective consequence, such as the defense of a stronger reversal of the burden of proof or expanded contractual control. Even so, this consequence is usually drawn en bloc, from the global perception of a hostile environment, and not from the more precise stabilization of the specific gear of asymmetry.<1>p. 600</1>

Evidence no longer gravitates only around the consumer's narrative and comes to require preservation of trails, verifiable transparency and rational redistribution of the burden of proof.<1>p. 601</1>

This alternative rests on the doctrine of the microsystem. The treatise by Benjamin, Marques and Bessa, guided by the principle of procedural cooperation, places on the supplier the burden of proving compliance with its duties, because each party must contribute the elements that can most easily be required of it, without prejudice to reversal, and treats dynamic allocation and reversal as instruments of distributive justice in the face of the concentration of evidence in the supplier. The allocation of burdens thus gains its measure, because it responds to the concrete architecture of the case, and the more intense the private concentration of records, the greater the requirement of preservation, of delimited production and of verifiable justification.

Guided by the principle of procedural cooperation, the supplier bears the burden of proving compliance with its duties, since each party must contribute the elements that can most easily be required of it, without prejudice to the reversal of the burden of proof <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 131])</2>.<3>p. 658-659</3>
Dynamic allocation and reversal of the burden of proof work as indispensable instruments of distributive justice in the face of the concentration of evidence on the supplier's side.<1>p. 659</1>

The dynamic allocation of burdens must, in this context, respond to the concrete architecture of the case. The more intense the private concentration of records, the greater the requirement of preservation, of delimited production and of verifiable justification.<1>p. 736</1>

On one point the CDC itself already allocates the burden. Article 38 of the CDC<1><2>12</2></1> assigns to whoever sponsors the advertising information or communication the burden of proving its truthfulness and correctness, and in this lies the normative recognition that advertising is a space of power and of responsibility. In IOCs, the provision prevents the consumer from having to prove alone that the expectation produced by the communication was incompatible with the actual regime of enjoyment.
The system does not presume the innocence of the marketing promise.<1>p. 627</1>

The burden of proving the truthfulness and correctness of the advertising information or communication lies with whoever sponsors it. This is not an elegant evidentiary detail. It is normative recognition that advertising is a space of power and, therefore, of responsibility. In IOCs, this provision prevents the consumer from having to prove alone that the expectation produced by the communication was incompatible with the actual regime of enjoyment.<1>p. 627</1>
What does the redistribution of the burden not dispense with?

Redistribution has a precondition. It responds to the scenario in which the consumer was placed in a situation of impossible or disproportionately difficult proof because the architecture of the environment concentrates, hides or volatilizes the relevant elements. It does not eliminate, however, the need for plausibility, for argumentative chaining and for delimiting the disputed object, and what is eliminated is the fiction of symmetry.

If the consumer was placed in a scenario of impossible or disproportionately difficult proof because the architecture of the environment concentrates, hides or volatilizes the relevant elements of the conflict, the evidentiary discipline needs to react to this asymmetry.<1>p. 735</1>

The more the reconstruction of the conflict depends on internal governance, the less reasonable it will be to require from the consumer a detailed demonstration of facts whose documentary and technical support was never within the consumer's reach. This does not eliminate the need for plausibility, argumentative chaining or delimitation of the disputed object. What it eliminates is the fiction of symmetry in environments whose very structure operates through the asymmetry of meaning and of evidence.<1>p. 736</1>

The qualification framework gives the measure of each side. From the consumer a plausible presentation of the harmful experience, of the consumer's insertion in the ecosystem and of the accessible context elements is required, and from the supplier, production of trails, logs, histories, versions and technically delimited justifications. The presumptions keep their modal, since the unjustified failure to preserve or produce relevant records may authorize presumptions favorable to the consumer and reinforce the imputation of inadequacy of the supply regime. The parameter also has a preventive function, because it discourages the convenient volatilization of the system's memory and selectively insufficient documentation.

The minimum evidence required, from the consumer's point of view, consists of a plausible presentation of the harmful experience, of the consumer's insertion in the ecosystem and of the accessible context elements; from the supplier's point of view, production of trails, logs, histories, versions and technically delimited justifications is required. The possible legal qualification involves dynamic redistribution of the burden of proof, presumptions favorable to the consumer and reinforcement of the duty of cooperation, without prejudice to the substantive application of the other parameters.<1>p. 747</1>

This parameter also has a preventive function. By recognizing that essential records form part of the controllability of the bond, it encourages the institutional organization of minimum reconstruction trails, discouraging governance models based on the convenient volatilization of the system's memory or on selectively insufficient documentation.<1>p. 736</1>

The unjustified failure to preserve or produce relevant records should not, therefore, be treated as a mere neutral evidentiary inconvenience. It may authorize presumptions favorable to the consumer and reinforce the imputation of inadequacy of the supply regime.<1>p. 736</1>
How do expert evidence and the remedy close the reconstruction?

The fourth mechanism is expert evidence oriented to functional impact, and not to the total engineering of the ecosystem. It should not become an endless audit nor require full disclosure of source code, architecture or trade secrets, and its object is delimited by what changed and by the extent to which this affected the utility, compatibility, continuity, position in the ecosystem or functional equivalence of the object, on the basis of minimum records, versions and preserved trails. Trade secrets may justify containing exposure, but not an absolute veto on reconstructing what the platform did when it became litigious, a topic the chapter on auditability develops.
The proceeding does not need to become a complete autopsy of the system; it only needs to be able to answer, with method, the legally right question.<1>p. 661</1>

The fourth mechanism is technical expert evidence oriented to functional impact, and not to the total engineering of the ecosystem. When the dispute requires specialized examination, expert evidence need not and should not turn into an endless audit of the platform, nor into a requirement of full disclosure of source code, architecture or trade secrets. Its object must be delimited by the legally relevant effects of the supply: what changed, to what extent this affected the utility, compatibility, continuity, ecosystemic position or functional equivalence of the IOC. Expert evidence comes in as a tool to close the reconstruction, operating on minimum records, relevant versions, preserved trails and verifiable functional parameters.<1>p. 661</1>
Trade secrets may justify containing exposure; they cannot function as an absolute veto on reconstructing what the platform did when that doing became legally litigious.<1>p. 661</1>

The fifth mechanism is the remedy, and the operationalization of the criteria should not automatically lead to damages, because the microsystem prioritizes specific performance, a practical result equivalent to performance and material restoration of the utility, and Miragem treats conversion into damages as subsidiary. Among the remedies are reversal of a relevant change, re-performance, restoration or maintenance of access, preservation of history, restoration of ecosystem or reputation attributes, equivalent functional substitution, alternative versions, correction of parameters and proportional compensation when full restoration is not feasible. The order among them is left to the chapter on remedies.

The fifth mechanism concerns remedies and protection proper. Here the central point is that the operationalization of open auditability and functional equivalence should not automatically lead to damages as the default solution. The consumer microsystem prioritizes specific performance, measures capable of ensuring a practical result equivalent to performance and material restoration of the contracted utility <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 856; p. 897)</2>. In IOCs, this means that the standards need to guide remedies aimed at restoring the functional and, where appropriate, symbolic integrity of enjoyment. Among these remedies are reversal of a relevant change, re-performance of the obligation, restoration or maintenance of access, preservation of history, restoration of ecosystemic or reputational attributes, equivalent functional substitution, mitigation through alternative versions, correction of parameters and proportional compensation when full restoration is not feasible <3>Miragem</3><4>(Miragem, 2020, p. 529-530)</4>.<5>p. 661-662</5>

The consumer system prioritizes specific performance or measures capable of ensuring the practical result equivalent to fulfillment of the obligation, admitting conversion into damages only on a subsidiary basis<1>p. 656</1>

When the dispute reveals a repeated pattern of opacity, abusive reconfiguration or unverifiable suppression of functional value, the response may take on a structural form, because on platforms unlawfulness usually comes in batches. The integration between the CDC and the Public Civil Action Law admits mandatory and executive orders, and the response may include a duty to preserve trails, a protocol of qualified communication, intelligible contestation procedures and minimum functional impact reports. The sixth mechanism, coordinated institutional action, carries the same criteria into conduct adjustment agreements, recommendations and civil investigations, without opening a parallel regulatory front.

When the dispute reveals a repeated pattern of opacity, abusive reconfiguration or unverifiable suppression of functional value, the response need not be limited to the individual case. It may take on a structural form: a duty to preserve minimum trails, to establish protocols for qualified communication of relevant changes, to organize intelligible contestation procedures, to maintain minimum functional impact reports or to adjust the supply regime to prevent the problem from recurring. This is especially important on platforms, where unlawfulness usually comes in batches, not as a single piece.<1>p. 662</1>

Through the integration between the CDC and the Public Civil Action Law, mandatory and executive orders capable of providing adequate and effective protection are admissible, ensuring that services are supplied adequately and, if essential, continuously <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 385; 783])</2>.<3>p. 657</3>

The sixth mechanism is coordinated institutional action. Without opening a parallel regulatory front, the subsection shows that open auditability and functional equivalence can also guide the action of protection bodies in platform markets. These standards offer a concrete criterion for conduct adjustment agreements, recommendations, civil investigations and minimum governance requirements: functional impact reports on relevant changes, protocols of verifiable transparency, preservation of essential records, understandable contestation procedures and minimum restoration criteria in case of relevant degradation of enjoyment.<1>p. 662-663</1>
How did a payment fraud become a problem of proof for those who received gifts?

The case of the irregular gifts shows how semiotic vulnerability can be converted into allegation, proof and consequence. Fraud, misuse of a means of payment and chargeback, which is the later contestation of the transaction, with bank reversal of the payment, are known risks in digital markets and, on their own, do not exhaust the relevance of the episode. The decisive point lies in the response of Riot Games, which, instead of treating the fraud as a structural problem of its own transactional environment, redistributed the risk to an undifferentiated mass of consumers, suppressed assets, interrupted the official gifting function and applied sanctions based on broad presumptions of co-responsibility, including against those who did not knowingly take part in the fraud.

What is here called the Case of the Irregular Gifts offers a particularly expressive example of how semiotic vulnerability can be converted into allegation, proof and consequence within the CDC. The interest of the episode does not lie only in the occurrence of financial fraud in the Riot Games ecosystem. Fraud, chargeback and misuse of a means of payment are known risks in digital markets and, by themselves, do not exhaust the legal relevance of the case.<1>p. 609-610</1>

The decisive point lies in the way the platform responded to this risk. Instead of treating the fraud as a structural problem of its own transactional environment, Riot redistributed the risk to an undifferentiated mass of consumers, suppressed assets, interrupted an official content circulation functionality and applied sanctions based on broad presumptions of co-responsibility, including against users who did not knowingly take part in the fraud.<1>p. 610</1>

The first layer is the institutional normality of the gift function, gifting. Riot itself presented it as a regular functionality, integrated into the game client, with objective eligibility requirements, such as minimum friendship time and account level, sending and receiving limits and specific restrictions for Brazil. This rules out the reading that consumers had entered, from the start, a manifestly unlawful zone, since confidence in the lawfulness of that channel was produced by the platform itself.

The ordinary official gifting regime in League of Legends is presented by Riot Games itself as a regular functionality, integrated into the game client and subject to objective formal eligibility requirements, such as minimum friendship time, account level, quantitative sending and receiving limits and specific restrictions for Brazil.<1>p. 610</1>

Gifting was part of the ordinary architecture of the service. The consumer's confidence in the lawfulness of the circulation of virtual content through this channel was not a subjective whim. It was confidence produced by the platform itself and supported by an officially offered functionality.<1>p. 610</1>

The second layer is the already known risk. Riot maintains, in League of Legends and in VALORANT, guidance on unauthorized charges, financial fraud and later contestation of transactions, with flows for investigation, refund, removal of payment data and account suspension. Chargeback was thus an operational risk recognized by the company, and whoever knows the fragility of its own transactional ecosystem cannot treat its effects as the consumer's residual fault, because the risk comes to form part of the professional circle of the economic operation.

The second layer is that of the operational risk already known to the supplier. Riot maintains, in more than one title of its portfolio, specific guidance for cases of unauthorized charges, financial fraud and later contestation of transactions. These communications show that the problem of chargeback and misuse of means of payment was not an external, extraordinary or unforeseeable fact. It was an institutionally recognized operational risk, with internal flows for investigation, refund and suspension.<1>p. 610</1>

Riot Games maintains specific guidance, both in League of Legends and in VALORANT, for cases of unauthorized charges, institutionally recognizing the occurrence of misuse of means of payment, financial fraud and later contestation of transactions in its monetization ecosystem <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2023e; Riot Games, 2023f)</2>. In both cases, the company provides formal incident response flows, with investigation of the fraud, refund of purchases, removal of payment data and suspension of the account linked to the contested operations <3>Riot Games</3><4>(Riot Games, 2023e; Riot Games, 2023f)</4>.<5>p. 610-611</5>

When the supplier already knows the fragility of the transactional ecosystem, it cannot treat its effects as if they were the consumer's residual fault or an accident wholly exogenous to the activity. The risk comes to form part of the professional circle of the economic operation itself.<1>p. 611</1>

It is the response that makes the case legally problematic. The company disabled the gift function on the Brazilian server for a long period, suppressed received assets and carried out regressive restorations or blocks, with no equivalent effort visible, in the private policy, to distinguish among intentional fraud, excusable error, acquisition through an apparently trustworthy channel and the recipient's good faith. Users perceived the restriction, since 2020, as a lasting functional amputation, with institutional silence, occasional reintroductions and new suppressions. These reports call for care, because they are not the central proof of an unlawful act and serve to formulate and illustrate a long-running consumer experience, even if hypothetical.

The company disabled the gifting functionality on the Brazilian server for a long period, suppressed received assets and carried out regressive restorations or blocks on affected accounts, with no equivalent effort visible, at the level of private policy, of consistent individualization among intentional fraud, excusable error, acquisition through an apparently trustworthy channel and the recipient's good faith. The restriction was perceived by users, since 2020, not as a brief and proportional measure, but as a lasting functional amputation, accompanied by institutional silence, occasional reintroductions and new suppressions. The community reports are not the central proof of an unlawful act, but they are useful to formulate and illustrate a, even if hypothetical, long-running consumer experience in which one glimpses the restriction and sedimentation of a broad punitive policy over the Brazilian base.<1>p. 611</1>

The private imputation was also built on a scrambled communicational field, and that is why the case matters for semiotic vulnerability. Promotional materials and digital storefronts presented the external purchase of Riot Points, the game's virtual currency, and of codes as an ordinary, safe practice compatible with the ecosystem, one of them with a video tutorial that advertised it as the best method, one hundred percent safe, and another with a professional storefront that displayed the Riot brand. In this environment, it is not legally serious to presume that the average consumer would always distinguish a tolerated partner, legitimate resale, gray market and fraud linked to a cloned card.

From the standpoint of semiotic vulnerability, the case is especially fertile because it shows that the private imputation was not built only on a raw financial fact, but also on a scrambled communicational field. The consumer did not face a simple distinction between an official channel and a flagrantly fraudulent channel. The market for Riot Points and external codes was crossed by a semiotic gray zone, in which promotional materials and digital storefronts presented the external purchase of virtual currency as an ordinary, safe, advantageous practice compatible with the game's ecosystem.<1>p. 611-612</1>

In one case, the sale is turned into a video tutorial as the “best method” to buy RP in a “100% safe” way, with a step-by-step of purchase, payment and activation of the code in the official client; in the other, the sale appears in a structured digital storefront, with professional presentation of the product, display of the Riot brand and the typical organization of legitimate retail of game content <1>fonte · ZERO3GAMES</1><2>(Como…, 2024a; Zero3Games, [202-?])</2>.<3>p. 612</3>

The language used in these environments mimicked commercial legitimacy, visual professionalism, later functional integration with the official client, plausible promises of savings and a rhetoric of safety. In this setting, it is not legally serious to presume that the average consumer would always distinguish, with sufficient clarity, a tolerated partner, legitimate resale, gray market and fraud linked to a cloned card.<1>p. 612</1>

Riot's chargeback policy aggravates the picture. In an official document, the company states that bank reversal authorizes suspension of the Riot Account until full reimbursement, with possible permanent ban in case of recurrence, and extends the effect to gift operations, reaching both who sent and who received. Purchases made by third parties, even when perceived by the consumer as legitimate, do not rule out the imputation of the debt and the sanction. Most problematic is that the policy reveals no prior requirement of robust individualization of the recipient's conduct and does not distinguish conscious fraud from receipt in a context of apparent legitimacy, so that the risk of financial reversal is converted into blocking and functional confiscation for the benefit of the supplier's economic recovery.
The consumer comes to function as a shock absorber for the systemic failure of the environment.<1>p. 613</1>

In a specific official policy, the company states that bank reversal authorizes suspension of the Riot Account until full reimbursement, and may even give rise to permanent ban in case of recurrence, and extends the sanctioning effect also to gift operations, reaching not only who sent but also who received the content.<1>p. 612</1>

The most expressive point, for this item, is that the company extends the sanctioning impact also to gift operations, providing for suspension of both the account that sent and the one that received the content, without the wording of the policy setting out any prior requirement of robust individualization of the recipient's conduct. The same guidance also makes clear that purchases made by third parties, even when perceived by the consumer as legitimate, do not rule out the imputation of the debt and the subsequent sanction.<1>p. 612</1>

The most problematic fact is that the policy reveals no prior requirement of robust individualization of the recipient's conduct, nor does it convincingly distinguish situations of conscious fraud from receipt in a context of apparent legitimacy. The risk of financial reversal, therefore, is converted into a mechanism of blocking and functional confiscation for the benefit of the supplier's economic recovery.<1>p. 612-613</1>
What do the clauses of the Terms of Service support, and why are they not enough?

The shifting of risk rests on a set of clauses that seek to lower the legal density of enjoyment. Clause 3.1 treats the use of the services and of virtual content as a limited, non-transferable and revocable license, canceled upon termination of the account. The central dogmatic point is that this contractual vocabulary is not enough to turn the consumer into the legitimate bearer of systemic risk. The CDC also protects the confidence aroused by the way the service is organized and by the functionalities placed on the market, and Marques argues that the rules of the CDC reach the entire chain of suppliers involved in satisfying the legitimate expectations of consumers, a chain that a revocable license clause does not erase. The platform that institutionalizes the functionality, knows the risks and lets the circulation of value run in an objectively confusing environment cannot treat the consumer as the universal guarantor of the system's failures.

What allegations and requests does the case allow one to formulate?

The episode reveals how the law of the platform can operate on three levels at once. It produces a semiotic gray zone in the circulation of value, without robust distinctions among the lawful, the tolerated and the unlawful, it unilaterally reorganizes the ecosystem in the face of the crisis and redistributes the risk onto consumers, and it uses the language of the revocable license and of limitation of liability to justify the retrospective precarization of enjoyment. The result is a private regime of imputation in which the supplier alone defines who bears the costs when the system fails.

The relevance of the case, then, goes beyond the historical episode. It shows how the Lex Plataformae can operate on three simultaneous levels. First, it produces a semiotic gray zone in the circulation of value, without sufficiently robust communicational distinctions among the lawful, the tolerated and the unlawful. Second, in the face of the crisis, it unilaterally reorganizes the ecosystem and redistributes the risk onto consumers. Third, it uses the language of revocable license, absence of property and limitation of liability to justify the retrospective precarization of enjoyment. The result is a private regime of imputation in which the supplier not only controls the environment and its risks, but also unilaterally defines who bears the costs when the system fails.<1>p. 617</1>

In dogmatic terms, the case allows five allegations to be formulated. The first is inadequacy of the service due to failure in the security and governance of the transactional environment, with later abusive redistribution of the risk. The second is violation of legitimate confidence, because the platform itself offered gifting as an ordinary and institutionalized channel. The third is abusiveness of the private response, through expanded presumption of bad faith and absence of reliable individualization of conduct. The fourth is ineffectiveness, in the concrete case, of the clauses used to turn enjoyment into absolutely precarious tolerance and to deny restoration. The fifth is evidentiary asymmetry, which calls for preservation of trails, transaction histories, origin of the removed items, rollback criteria and individualized justification of the measures.

The first and most corrosive is that the consumer has not proved it, which converts the consumer's lack of access into absence of proof of the right itself. In these environments, the absence of proof may be less a weakness of the claim and more a result of the supplier's governance arrangement, and the law cannot accept that the platform administers at the same time the enjoyment, the narrative of the event and the conditions of its verifiability.

Can the consumer demand to see everything?

The discipline of evidence does not protect the consumer's technological curiosity, but the institutional possibility of reconstructing changes and impacts that affect enjoyment, so the request is guided by the reconstruction of these impacts. It also exists for the sake of the substantive criteria, because it is not enough to state that changes must be intelligible or that enjoyment must remain equivalent, and it is evidence that makes modulations, losses, reconfigurations and sanctions demonstrable and contestable. Without it, auditability and equivalence would remain correct in the abstract and ineffective in practice, and that is why evidence is not an accessory stage of the reasoning, but a means of effectiveness of the regime itself.
What is protected here is not the consumer's technological curiosity, but the institutional possibility of reconstructing changes and impacts that affect the consumer's enjoyment.<1>p. 661</1>

The evidentiary discipline proposed here is also important because it prevents standards such as open auditability and functional value equivalence from turning into mere conceptual rhetoric. Without a compatible evidentiary regime, these parameters would remain correct in theory, but ineffective in practice.<1>p. 736</1>

It is not enough to state that relevant changes must be intelligible or that enjoyment must remain functionally equivalent. There must be instruments to demonstrate, contest and reconstruct the occurrence of modulations, losses, reconfigurations and sanctions. Evidence, therefore, is not a later and accessory stage of the reasoning. It is a means of effectiveness of the regime itself.<1>p. 736</1>

Why does a money award usually fail in the face of governed enjoyment?

The system's reflex in the face of a consumer injury is to convert it into compensation. This solution, often necessary, is not rejected, but it frequently proves insufficient when what is at stake is not only the immediate economic loss, but the degradation, interruption or abusive reconfiguration of a continuous enjoyment, governed and situated within an ecosystem. In these bonds, later payment may leave the harmful mechanism untouched, preserve the architecture that produced the problem and normalize the repetition of the loss as an ordinary cost of the supply model.

The legal response to conflicts involving the Immaterial Object of Consumption cannot be organized on the basis of the traditional automatism of converting the injury into pecuniary compensation. This solution, although often necessary, frequently proves insufficient when what is at stake is not only the immediate economic loss, but the degradation, interruption or abusive reconfiguration of a continuous enjoyment, governed and functionally situated within an ecosystem.<1>p. 739</1>

The second lies in what money leaves standing. When the injury is architectural, repeatable and built into ordinary operation, merely compensatory protection tends to operate as a manageable cost of the business model, and treating every injury of this kind as compensable in money means, in many cases, accepting that the supplier may degrade enjoyment and then merely internalize the price. The rule is direct. Whenever technically and legally feasible, priority protection should seek the functional restoration of enjoyment and the correction of the regime that made it inadequate. The primacy does not derive from an abstract preference for specific performance nor from ritual attachment to restoration in natura, but from the structure of the bond. If the utility consumed is an immaterial experience maintained by continuous governance, the relevant injury tends to fall on access, continuity, integrity, equivalence, intelligibility, history, relational position or the consumer's insertion in the environment, and restoration corresponds better to the nature of the legal interest affected. In objects of high identity, historical or reputational density, setting a sum also runs the risk of treating as equivalent what, in practice, is not.

Article 18 of the CDC<1><2>3</2></1> therefore remains the central gateway for framing a relevant defect in a continuous environment, now read by the yardstick of functional equivalence and not only by the classic image of the spoiled product on the shelf.<3>p. 562</3>

In case of a defect, the CDC allows the consumer to demand another product of the same kind in perfect conditions of use, alongside restitution or a proportional reduction of the price <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 338])</2>.<3>p. 563</3>

This logic appears even more concretely in Article 20 of the CDC<1><2>4</2></1>. In the face of quality defects that reduce the value of the service, the consumer may demand contractual rescission without penalty or a proportional reduction of the price, without needing to discuss the supplier's fault, since this is strict liability <3>Bessa</3><4>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 354])</4>.<5>p. 563</5>

In the regime of defects, the priority given to replacing the product or service with another in perfect conditions of use reveals that adequate protection seeks the concrete recovery of the utility that motivated the contract, and not merely the symbolic satisfaction of pecuniary compensation <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 529-530])</2>.<3>p. 662</3>

The orientation fits in three conditionals. The remedy aims at enjoyment when the bond is one of governed enjoyment, reaches the structure when the injury is structural and restores the function when the loss is functional. Without this, the regime would be merely a sophisticated grammar of diagnosis, without real transformative force.

If the bond is one of governed enjoyment, the remedy must aim at enjoyment. If the injury is structural, protection must reach the structure. If the loss is functional, the priority response must be functionally restorative.<1>p. 742</1>
Only in this way does the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption avoid being reduced to a sophisticated grammar of diagnosis without real transformative force.<1>p. 742</1>
What are the remedies and in what order?

Functional restoration is not a single remedy, but a set of possible measures, calibrated according to the structure of the impaired enjoyment. The main list runs from restoration of access and review of sanctions to preservation of history, reactivation of functionalities, substitution by a functionally equivalent position, reversibility of versions when technically possible and procedural corrections, such as verifiable reasoning and intelligible contestation. In the operation of auditability and equivalence, re-performance of the obligation, restoration of ecosystemic or reputational attributes, mitigation through alternative versions, correction of parameters and proportional compensation when full restoration is not feasible are added. In the conclusion, reversal of relevant degradations, cessation of opaque or exploitative practices and minimum standards of verifiability come in. The list is open, and the three versions are read together.

Functional restoration, in this context, comprises a set of possible measures, calibrated according to the structure of the impaired enjoyment. It may involve maintenance or restoration of access, reversal or review of sanctions, preservation of history, reactivation of functionalities, substitution by a functionally equivalent position, reversibility of versions when technically possible, procedural corrections of governance, duties of verifiable reasoning, intelligible contestation mechanisms and other means capable of substantially reestablishing the utility legitimately incorporated into the bond.<1>p. 740</1>

The consumer microsystem prioritizes specific performance, measures capable of ensuring a practical result equivalent to performance and material restoration of the contracted utility <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 856; p. 897)</2>. In IOCs, this means that the standards need to guide remedies aimed at restoring the functional and, where appropriate, symbolic integrity of enjoyment. Among these remedies are reversal of a relevant change, re-performance of the obligation, restoration or maintenance of access, preservation of history, restoration of ecosystemic or reputational attributes, equivalent functional substitution, mitigation through alternative versions, correction of parameters and proportional compensation when full restoration is not feasible <3>Miragem</3><4>(Miragem, 2020, p. 529-530)</4>.<5>p. 661-662</5>

Whenever technically and legally possible, protection must aim at enjoyment, and not only at its later monetary translation. This means favoring functional restoration, reestablishment of access, reversal of relevant degradations, regime correction, cessation of opaque or exploitative practices and imposition of minimum standards of verifiability on changes that substantially affect the acquired object.<1>p. 797</1>

The criterion that calibrates the choice is not the literal reproduction of the prior state at any cost, but the functionally adequate restitution of the injured experience, at a level compatible with what the consumer had legitimately incorporated into their sphere of enjoyment. The yardstick is functional value equivalence, which also serves to guide remedies, and which the chapter on equivalence examines.
It does not serve only to identify unlawfulness. It also serves to guide remedies.<1>p. 731</1>

The order of preference is clear. First comes functional restoration, whenever technically and legally feasible, and when the injury is structural regime correction is added to it, since together the two form priority protection. Then comes compensation, which remains legitimate and, in many cases, indispensable, but takes on a residual or complementary nature whenever restoration is unfeasible, insufficient or unable to cover the losses in full, and it continues to redress material losses and to recognize non-pecuniary damages when present. The qualification framework repeats the order by directing that restoration be prioritized whenever the injury affects access, continuity, equivalence, history, relational position or the meaningful density of enjoyment, reserving compensation for when restoration is unfeasible or insufficient.
Pecuniary compensation remains necessary in many cases, but it cannot occupy, by automatism, the position of sovereign remedy.<1>p. 797</1>

Pecuniary compensation remains, of course, a legitimate and in many cases indispensable remedy. The parameter formulated here does not eliminate it. It merely places it in a systematically more precise position. It takes on a residual or complementary nature whenever functional restoration is unfeasible, insufficient or unable to cover in full the losses suffered.<1>p. 741-742</1>
In these cases, monetary compensation continues to play an important role, whether to redress material losses or to recognize non-pecuniary damages when present.<1>p. 742</1>
What separates restoring the case from correcting the regime?

Restoring the case and correcting the regime answer different questions. Functional restoration looks at the injured consumer and seeks to reestablish the position of enjoyment the consumer had legitimately incorporated. Regime correction looks at the arrangement that produced the injury. It opens up when the injury is architectural, repeatable and built into ordinary supply, because then the problem is no longer only the loss of a particular consumer and comes to lie in the permanence of an arrangement capable of repeating the same inadequacy indefinitely. The remedies of this second plane address the continuous source of the problem, such as the reconfiguration of flows, procedural duties, review of sanction mechanisms, verifiable reasoning and intelligible contestation channels.

The problem then ceases to be only the loss suffered by a particular consumer and comes to lie in the permanence of a harmful arrangement capable of reproducing the same inadequacy indefinitely.<1>p. 741</1>

The parameter therefore opens room for regime correction. This means admitting, when the case reveals a structural pattern of abusiveness, remedies aimed at the reconfiguration of flows, the imposition of procedural duties, the review of sanction mechanisms, the requirement of verifiable reasoning, the creation of intelligible contestation channels and other measures capable of reaching the continuous source of the problem.<1>p. 741</1>

The difference is also one of time. Restoration repairs a loss already suffered, while correction is directed at the mode of operation that made the injury ordinary and at the future conditions of control of enjoyment. Treating the case only as an isolated event loses sight of the repeatability of the harm. Regime correction reconnects individual protection to the collective dimension, which may justify injunctive relief, structural measures, collective measures and even mechanisms of compulsory compliance, that is, compliance programs imposed on the supplier, compatible with open auditability.

When the problem stems from continuous, repeatable and structural governance, protection also needs to be conceived in functional and structural terms. This requires going beyond later compensation and considering remedies capable of restoring the experience, interrupting the reiteration of the harmful mechanism and correcting the mode of operation that made the injury ordinary.<1>p. 740</1>
This opening is particularly relevant because it reconnects individual protection to the collective and institutional dimension of the IOC regime.<1>p. 741</1>

Treating the case exclusively as an isolated event means losing sight of the repeatability of the harm and of the environment's capacity to produce the same injury in series. Regime correction, by contrast, allows the harm to be treated as architectural and not only as an episode. This makes it possible to justify injunctive relief, structural measures, collective measures and even mechanisms of compulsory compliance compatible with open auditability and institutional control of enjoyment.<1>p. 741</1>
[...] and other measures that are not directed only at repairing past harm, but at reorganizing the future conditions of controllability of enjoyment.<1>p. 775</1>

The boundary between the two planes does not run through the type of measure. Verifiable reasoning and intelligible contestation channels appear both in the list of restoration and in that of regime correction, which indicates that the same measure can serve both planes. What changes is the object and the precondition. Correction requires that the case reveal a structural pattern, or, in the words of the guidelines, a repeated, replicable pattern built into the structure of the environment. When abusive teleology is recognized, the remedial horizon widens in the same direction, because, if the abusiveness lies in the program, it is not enough to treat the isolated effects, and injunctive relief, reconfiguration of flows, review of selective frictions, duties of reasoning and more symmetrical reversibility mechanisms become available.

When the pattern of injury proves repeated, replicable and built into the structure of the environment, protection should not be limited to the single case. Room opens for injunctive relief and for measures of regime correction.<1>p. 751</1>

If the abusiveness lies in the program, it is not enough to treat its isolated effects. It becomes appropriate to consider injunctive relief, reconfiguration of flows, review of selective frictions, duties of reasoning, more symmetrical reversibility mechanisms, adjustments of informational visibility and other measures capable of reaching the architecture as the continuous source of the problem.<1>p. 733-734</1>

On the procedural plane, specific enforcement under Article 84 of the CDC<1><2>2</2></1> serves to achieve the practical result equivalent to performance, and the treatise by Benjamin, Marques and Bessa highlights the imposition of daily fines as a means of producing the due result and discouraging deliberate breach based on economic calculation. Through the integration between the CDC and the Public Civil Action Law, the same treatise admits mandatory and executive orders. Individual protection, however, does not dissolve into structural protection. It remains indispensable to repair losses concretely experienced, and a merely atomized treatment tends to monetize episodes without altering the machine that reproduces them.

Declarations of will contained in private writings, receipts and preliminary contracts bind the supplier and their breach may give rise to specific enforcement under art. 84, precisely to achieve the “practical result equivalent to that of performance” of the obligation <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 597])</2>.<3>p. 563</3>

In actions for the performance of obligations, the discipline of specific enforcement takes on special importance, including with the imposition of daily fines, as a means of producing the due material result and discouraging deliberate breach based on economic calculation <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 111])</2>. Through the integration between the CDC and the Public Civil Action Law, mandatory and executive orders capable of providing adequate and effective protection are admissible, ensuring that services are supplied adequately and, if essential, continuously <3>Bessa</3><4>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 385; 783])</4>.<5>p. 657</5>

This does not mean abolishing the role of individual protection. It remains indispensable, above all for redress of losses concretely experienced and for the situated reconstruction of certain specific impacts.<1>p. 775</1>
A merely atomized treatment of the conflict tends to produce two bad results. On one side, it monetizes episodes without altering the machine that reproduces them.<1>p. 776</1>
Where does the remedy come into the sequence of the examination?

There are three similar sequences, and confusing them produces apparent contradictions. The first has four steps and guides the application of the parameters and the presentation of the platform families, from the governance mechanism and the friction it produces to the central vulnerability, from there to the standard of proof and, finally, to the possible dogmatic consequence. The second orders the statements as a staged decision sequence, with the qualification of the object, semiotic vulnerability, the duties of information and advertising, open auditability, functional value equivalence, abusive teleology and the allocation of evidentiary burdens and, at the end, intellectual property and restoration. The third is the qualification framework, which operates through cumulative filters and only qualifies the dispute after identifying the object, qualifying the vulnerability and verifying opacity, mutability and governance by sanction, with auditability and equivalence as cross-cutting filters.
To maintain this comparability, the presentation will follow a constant sequence.<1>p. 756</1>

The statements should not be read as a horizontal inventory of concepts. Their function is to organize a staged decision sequence, in which each parameter prepares the application of the next and limits the field of interpretive variation of the subsequent step.<1>p. 716-717</1>
Open auditability, functional value equivalence, abusive teleology and rational allocation of evidentiary burdens operate as criteria of verification, containment and imputation.<1>p. 717</1>

The framework operates through cumulative filters. It starts from the identification of the IOC and of the regime of governed enjoyment. Next, semiotic vulnerability is qualified and, as the case may be, structural opacity, relevant mutability and governance by sanction are verified. Open auditability and functional value equivalence operate as cross-cutting filters, applying to different forms of conflict. Only then does one proceed to the legal qualification of the dispute, without prejudice to cumulation when the same arrangement reveals, simultaneously, relevant inadequacy of supply and repeated exploitation of vulnerability.<1>p. 742-743</1>

The three order different things, the reading of a conflict, the parameters and the qualification, and they converge at the point that matters for the remedy. In the second, evidence comes after abusive teleology, and the passage on restoration repeats this order when listing what precedes it. In the first, teleology does not appear as a step of its own, because the same passage places it among the legitimacy filters that operate on the base formed by the object and the vulnerability, and evidence is the third step. In the framework, each situation sets out the minimum evidence before the qualification and the consequence. In none of the three does the consequence come before the evidence.
On this base, the legitimacy filters built on the dogmatic plane come into operation, with centrality for open auditability, functional value equivalence and abusive teleology.<1>p. 715-716</1>

This parameter thus fulfills the function of closing the regime. Once the object is recognized, the vulnerability identified, the duties of information and advertising controlled, auditability required, functional equivalence assessed, any abusive teleology ascertained and evidence organized in an environment of structural opacity, the decisive question arises of what to do with the conflict.<1>p. 740</1>

The remedy also has its own evidence. The qualification framework requires demonstration of the link between the governance mechanism and the functional loss and of the technical or institutional possibility of restoration, reversal, equivalent substitution or procedural correction. The legal qualification varies according to the main incidence of the case, but the consequence should favor restoration of access, reversal of sanctions, preservation of history, equivalent substitution, governance adjustments, injunctive relief and structural correction when the harm reveals a repeatable pattern. The last of the guidelines asks, in the same vein, for unity among supply, evidence and remedy, since the way the architecture distributes access and opacity influences the adequacy of the response.

The possible legal qualification varies according to the main incidence of the case, but the institutional consequence should favor restoration of access, reversal of sanctions, preservation of history, equivalent functional substitution, governance adjustments, injunctive relief and structural correction when the harm reveals a repeatable pattern.<1>p. 748</1>
The way the architecture distributes access and opacity influences the adequacy of the remedy.<1>p. 751</1>
How are the three passages on the closing of the regime reconciled?

The vocabulary of closing appears three times. Compatibility with intellectual property and the primacy of restoration are necessary operational closures, the first because it defines the limit of private exclusivity in the face of consumer protection and the second because it defines the legally adequate form of response to the conflict. Abusive teleology is a closing category of the regime of controllability. And the restoration parameter fulfills the function of closing the regime.

Compatibility with intellectual property and the primacy of functional restoration appear, at the end, as necessary operational closures, defining, on one side, the limit of private exclusivity in the face of consumer protection and, on the other, the legally adequate form of response to the conflict.<1>p. 717</1>

That is why abusive teleology functions as a closing category of the regime of controllability. Once the object is qualified, the vulnerability identified, the duties of information and advertising assessed, auditability required and functional equivalence tested, it becomes possible to ask whether the environment as a whole reveals only legitimate governance or already operates as a program of exploitation built into enjoyment itself.<1>p. 734</1>

The three passages are reconciled when one observes that each closes a different question. Abusive teleology closes the diagnosis, because, once auditability is required and equivalence tested, it asks whether the environment reveals legitimate governance or a program of exploitation. Intellectual property closes the limit, because it says how far exclusivity can resist control, and the qualification framework subjects its exercise to the duties of adequacy, transparency and restoration. Restoration closes the whole regime, because it asks what to do with the conflict. The comparison between the lists of antecedents reinforces the reading, since the list that precedes teleology stops at equivalence, while the one that precedes restoration includes teleology and evidence. The closures also communicate, because, when the diagnosis ends in a program, the architecture becomes an unlawful act and the response cannot be neutral toward it.

The institutional consequence consists in making exclusivity and consumer protection compatible through delimited auditability, control of functional equivalence and subjection of the exercise of IP to the duties of adequacy, transparency and restoration.<1>p. 747-748</1>
When the answer is the second, the architecture ceases to be a backdrop and becomes an unlawful act.<1>p. 734</1>
The response cannot be neutral toward the architecture of the injury.<1>p. 740</1>
What can be requested when the closing of the account erases the consumer's trajectory?

The problem appears clearly in the account termination clause of the Riot Games Terms of Service. Once the account is terminated, the user loses access to it, to the associated data, to the game currency and to the virtual content, without refund when there is just cause, and may have other accounts and access to other services canceled. The clause lays the problem bare, because what is lost is not an isolated item, but the overall position of enjoyment, the history, the inventory, the trajectory and the continuity of insertion in the ecosystem, and exclusivity appears exercised as a power of total erasure of the experience consumed. That is why the sanction, the deletion or the rollback, which is the reversion of the account to an earlier state, cannot be treated as mere internal adjustments without existential legal relevance. The text of the clause itself notes that termination does not limit the user's rights under data protection and consumer protection laws.

Clause 2.3 of Riot's Terms of Service provides that, once the account is terminated, the user loses access to the account, to the associated data, to the game currency and to the virtual content, without refund in cases of just cause, with the further possibility of cancellation of other accounts and of access to other services.<1>p. 540</1>

The response begins with restoration. In long-lasting objects, Articles 35 and 84 of the CDC<1><2>5</2></1> place the restoration of the position of enjoyment before redress, and the platform's contractual framework makes this point crucial. Erasures, resets, inventory deletions, suppressions of history and sanctions that eliminate the biography built in the environment require verifiable reasoning, minimum preservation of records and, where appropriate, restoration of the position of enjoyment. Restoration depends on the case, and the first two requirements do not depend on it.
This point is crucial in view of the platform's own contractual framework.<1>p. 540</1>

The regime also offers procedural and access remedies. If the platform administers access, permanence, visibility, sanctions and participation trails, it also administers inclusion and exclusion in the digital social space, and from this follow minimum parameters of private due process, with verifiable reasoning, decisional coherence, procedural predictability and intelligible avenues of contestation, which, when the exclusion follows a pattern, lend themselves to regime correction. The LGPD reinforces the picture, because Article 18 of the LGPD preserves for the data subject the rights of confirmation, access, correction, deletion and portability of the data processed. The parallel with Article 24, item VII, of the Copyright Law also holds, which grants the author the right to access a unique and rare copy of the work held by another in order to preserve its memory. The parallel does not turn the consumer into an author, and it shows that the legal system already admits, in another domain, minimum positive duties of access and of enabling a record.

At this point, the LGPD provides important reinforcements. The use of data linked to the consumer's trajectory, history and digital biography must remain compatible with the purposes informed and with the context of the relationship, must be intelligible to the data subject, and does not eliminate the rights of confirmation of existence, access, correction, deletion or portability of the data processed.<1>p. 542</1>

“Art. 18. The data subject has the right to obtain from the controller, in relation to the data subject's data processed by it, at any time and upon request: [I - confirmation of existence; II - access; III - correction; IV - anonymization/blocking/deletion; V - portability...]”<1>p. 542</1>

The Copyright Law recognizes, in art. 24, VII, the author's moral right to access a unique and rare copy of the work that is legitimately in the possession of another in order to preserve its memory. The point is not to convert the consumer into an author, nor to transplant the regime of moral copyright into the consumer field. The point is narrower and more elegant: the Brazilian legal system already admits, in another domain, that the preservation of memory linked to an immaterial object under the control of a third party may justify minimum positive duties of access and of enabling a record.<1>p. 542</1>

The picture has limits. The expression digital existential minimum does not serve to inflate any online discomfort into a constitutional drama, and designates only a core of stability and continuity that can be required in long-lasting objects with a high identity load, such as account, history, progression, reputation and inventory. The provisions of the LGPD, in turn, do not make the consumer the absolute owner of everything the platform records.
The administration of another's digital biography cannot operate as a sovereign black box.<1>p. 542</1>

When restoration is not enough, compensation comes in with its own density. In qualified cases, the loss of an account, history or trajectory may constitute moral damages for injury to personality, above all when it objectively affects biographical continuity, institutionalized belonging in the ecosystem or relevant anchors of reputation and memory, and not mere subjective annoyance. The methodological parallel with aesthetic damage, with support in the work of Teresa Ancona Lopez, is useful, because Brazilian law already knows categorical refinements that prevent injuries to the person from being swallowed by overly generic headings, which legitimizes greater analytical density for injuries to the digital trajectory.

What do the recurring patterns of friction, evidence and restoration show outside the game?

The tests carried out on other platform families show that the keys of the regime do not depend on the laboratory in which they were formulated. What distinct ecosystems have in common does not lie on the surface of the environment, but in the way enjoyment is governed, expectation is administered, intelligibility is modulated and contestation becomes more or less practicable by private design. This result takes the regime out of a merely inventive position and places it in a decidable one.

For the lawyer, the most useful thing is to know that the environment that governs enjoyment also governs the way frustration will be perceived, justified, proved and neutralized before it becomes an institutional conflict. In each family, the mechanism of harmful modulation, the evidentiary problem and the rationale of restoration need to be kept distinct, seen in connection, but not in collapse. The injury is not to be confused with its proof, the difficulty of proving is not to be confused with the injury, and adequate restoration is not automatically deduced from categories that treat every loss as monetizable. By keeping distinguishable, in each platform family, the mechanism of harmful modulation, the corresponding evidentiary problem and the rationale of restoration required by the regime, both empty abstraction and casuistic dispersion are avoided. The same passage draws the limit. What emerges from the models is not the conclusion that the IOC would serve for almost everything, and controllability does not depend on freezing innovation, imposing absolute transparency or turning the platform into a quasi-state entity. What emerges from the analysis of the models is not, therefore, the conclusion that the IOC would serve for almost everything.<1>p. 788</1>

Is restoration not impracticable in a technical environment?

The first is the objection from complexity, according to which specific performance would be impracticable in a technical and continuously changing environment. This is an undue reduction, because the architecture of the environment cannot serve as an automatic excuse for downgrading remedies. Complexity does not equal impossibility.<1>p. 741</1>

When full restoration is not feasible, the list of remedies itself provides for proportional compensation. What is rejected is automatism, that is, turning money into the preferred response in every case, as if every injury to the IOC could be translated into a figure without attention to the structure of the impaired enjoyment.

What does the regime deliver to the jurist?

The underlying question is to what extent the normative structure of the CDC offers adequate protection to consumers placed in continuous digital ecosystems, in which enjoyment depends on stable private governance, ordinary mutability and opaque decisions built into the architecture of supply. The difficulty does not lie in a lack of normative basis, but in an ontologically impoverished reading of the CDC itself. The legal system already has sufficient openness, provided that Article 3, paragraph 1, of the CDC<1><2>6</2></1> is reread with dogmatic density, and what was missing was not a new microsystem for the digital, but a conceptual reconstruction that would take the immaterial good out of the residual position in which it was kept.

Within this horizon, the central legal question of this research consisted in verifying to what extent the normative structure of the Consumer Protection Code offers adequate protection to consumers placed in continuous digital ecosystems, in which the enjoyment of what was acquired depends on stable private governance, ordinary mutability and opaque decisions built into the very architecture of supply.<1>p. 793</1>
